abstract: Gestational trophoblastic disease is a term that describes a group of tumors that share several characteristics as follows: (1) they arise in fetal chorion, (2) they produce human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), and (3) they respond extremely well to chemotherapy. Although rare, they have received a disproportionate amount of attention because they were the first metastatic solid tumor to be cured using chemotherapy. Also, hCG was the first reliable tumor marker. Finally, because they arise in fetal tissue, they have the potential for a strong immune response against paternal antigens in the tumor. This potential for immunologic rejection was thought initially to explain the success of chemotherapy in this disease. The early detection of gestational trophoblastic disease is successful in patients who have had a hydatidiform mole as the pregnancy event that begins the process but unsuccessful in the early detection of the development of choriocarcinoma after a normal term delivery, abortion (spontaneous or elective), or ectopic pregnancy. Surveillance after evacuation of a molar pregnancy (whether complete or a partial mole) consists of regular evaluation of hCG production and the detection of metastatic disease. However, the development of gestational choriocarcinoma after term pregnancy or an abortion (no molar tissue can develop as a consequence of these pregnancies) is detectable only by signs or symptoms of metastatic disease in any of the many organs to which this tissue can spread. Unlike most staging classifications in gynecologic cancers, which are based on histologic findings and tumor location, the classification used in gestational trophoblastic disease stresses other features that are more useful for treatment selection. Both the National Institutes of Health and the World Health Organization classifications emphasize the importance of recognizing factors that predict the likelihood of a tumor responding to chemotherapy. Currently available treatment can cure all patients except those who are in the very high-risk group, which usually is characterized by metastasis to the brain or liver or a history of prior chemotherapy. Even in this category, approximately 80% of patients are curable.
abstract_ja: 妊娠性絨毛性疾患とは、次の3つの特徴を共有する腫瘍群を指す用語である。(1)胎児の絨毛に由来する、(2)ヒト絨毛性ゴナドトロピン(hCG)を産生する、(3)化学療法に非常に良好に反応する。まれな疾患であるが、化学療法によって転移性固形腫瘍として初めて治癒した腫瘍であること、またhCGが最初の信頼できる腫瘍マーカーであったことから、不均衡なほど注目を集めてきた。さらに、胎児組織に由来するため、腫瘍内の父親由来抗原に対して強い免疫応答が起こりうる。当初、この免疫拒絶の可能性が化学療法の成功を説明するものと考えられていた。胞状奇胎を発端とする妊娠では早期発見が成功するが、正常満期分娩、流産(自然または人工)、子宮外妊娠の後に絨毛癌が発生した場合の早期発見は成功しない。胞状奇胎(完全または部分胞状奇胎)の除去後の経過観察は、hCG産生の定期的評価と転移の検出から成る。一方、正期産や流産後に発生する妊娠性絨毛癌は、この組織が広がりうる多くの臓器の転移症状によってのみ検出される。婦人科悪性腫瘍の病期分類の多くが組織学的所見と腫瘍の位置に基づくのとは異なり、妊娠性絨毛性疾患の分類は治療選択により有用な他の特徴を重視する。米国国立衛生研究所(NIH)と世界保健機関(WHO)の分類はいずれも、化学療法への反応性を予測する因子を認識することの重要性を強調している。現在利用可能な治療により、非常にリスクの高い群、通常は脳または肝臓への転移や化学療法歴を有する群を除くすべての患者を治癒させることができる。この群においても、約80%の患者は治癒可能である。
